title: Not Just Rock: 66-Million-Year-Old Dino Bone Yields Original Proteins
summary: The idea that dinosaur fossils are nothing but mineralized rock has been shaken. Researchers at the University of Liverpool have uncovered compelling evidence that original organic molecules—specifically collagen—survive in a 66-million-year-old Edmontosaurus bone. The finding, published in Analytical Chemistry, adds weight to a controversial hypothesis that has divided paleontologists for over three decades. The fossil, a 22-kilogram sacrum from South Dakota's Hell Creek Formation, was analyzed using protein sequencing and multiple forms of mass spectrometry. The team detected collagen, the primary structural protein in bone, along with hydroxyproline, an amino acid strongly associated with it. Professor Steve Taylor, who led the research, stated, "This research shows beyond doubt that organic biomolecules, such as proteins like collagen, appear to be present in some fossils." He emphasized that it refutes the assumption that any organics found must be contamination. The debate ignited in 2005 when Mary Schweitzer reported soft tissue in a T. rex fossil. Skeptics argued the materials were modern bacteria or lab contaminants. This new study stands out because it used multiple independent methods on the same specimen, cross-validating the results. By combining microscopy, chemical analysis, and protein sequencing, the team built a robust case that the molecules are endogenous—original to the dinosaur. The implications are profound. If proteins can persist for tens of millions of years, they open a new window into dinosaur biology. Scientists could potentially trace evolutionary relationships, growth patterns, and diseases that bones alone cannot reveal. Taylor noted that researchers may need to revisit fossil collections, as old microscopy images might contain overlooked evidence of preserved collagen. The discovery also poses a fascinating question: how did these fragile molecules survive? Possible mechanisms, such as mineral binding or rapid burial, are now under scrutiny. This breakthrough doesn't just rewrite paleontology—it invites us to re-examine every fossil with fresh eyes.
why_it_matters: By proving that original proteins can survive deep time, this breakthrough could transform how we study extinct species — and may even lead to medical insights from ancient molecules, similar to how studying ice-age DNA has advanced genetics.

background_read: The late Cretaceous Hell Creek Formation (a famous fossil site in South Dakota, about 66 million years old) has produced many dinosaur skeletons, but scientists long believed that only mineralized bone could survive that long. In 2005, paleontologist Mary Schweitzer shocked the field by reporting what looked like flexible blood vessels and cells in a T. rex fossil — a claim many dismissed as contamination from modern bacteria or lab handling.

The new study tackles those doubts head-on. Professor Steve Taylor (a chemist at the University of Liverpool who led the research) and his team used advanced tools like mass spectrometry and protein sequencing on an Edmontosaurus (a duck-billed dinosaur) sacrum from the same formation.

By cross-validating through multiple independent techniques, they showed the collagen molecules are truly ancient, not modern pollutants. This aligns with a broader shift in paleontology: fragile biomolecules can sometimes survive for tens of millions of years if protected by minerals or special burial conditions.
The discovery encourages scientists to re-examine museum collections for overlooked traces of original organic material.

perspectives.description: Paleontologists now have a tool to investigate dinosaur physiology, metabolism, and evolutionary relationships in ways bones alone never allowed. This could answer questions about warm-bloodedness, growth rates, and disease that fossils could only hint at before.

Some researchers still worry about contamination, and the rarity of such preservation means most fossils won’t yield useful proteins. Overhyping a single bone might distract from the fact that fossilization usually annihilates organics, and funding could shift away from traditional methods.

For most of paleontology’s history, the rule was that only mineralized remains survive deep time. This study solidifies a paradigm shift, much like the discovery of feathered dinosaurs changed our view of birds. It shows that science must keep questioning its assumptions, especially as technology improves.

Scientists will now revisit fossil collections worldwide with more sensitive instruments. If proteins are more common than thought, we may build molecular family trees of dinosaurs or detect disease markers — and the same techniques could be applied to specimens from other time periods, potentially rewriting evolutionary biology.
